The Angles and Saxons were Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries, progressively conquering Roman territories and establishing the foundation of English civilization. After the empire's departure, they settled the eastern and central regions of Britain, gradually displacing or absorbing the native Romano-British population. They established rival kingdoms including Northumbria, Mercia, Wessex, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and East Anglia—collectively called the Heptarchy. These kingdoms would dominate Britain for nearly five centuries. The Angles and Saxons maintained pagan religious practices longer than most Germanic peoples until missionaries like Augustine of Canterbury, sent by Pope Gregory, converted them to Christianity beginning around 600. Mercia and Wessex gradually emerged as the dominant powers, and Wessex eventually unified the kingdoms under Alfred the Great, who reigned from 871 to 899. As they established themselves, they developed sophisticated legal codes and administrative systems that blended Germanic custom with surviving Roman practices. The Anglo-Saxon period, roughly from 450 to 1066, became the foundation of English law, language, literature, and identity, ending only with the Norman Conquest. The Old English language they established and the legal traditions they created would define English civilization for centuries to come.
